newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French troops clash with Bangui mutineers.
newsitem.headline: French troops clash with Bangui mutineers.

text.p: French troops fought mutinous government soldiers in the capital of the Central African Republic on Thursday for the first time since a revolt by some army units erupted last month, reporters and residents said.
A correspondent for French radio in Bangui said French troops opened fire as rebels launched another attack on the centre of Bangui.

The manager of the Sofitel hotel, which came under rebel mortar fire, said French troops had taken up positions there and had asked to use the building's rooftop to get a better view of rebel positions.

Mortar bombs fell close to the hotel and many guests fled in the night, the manager said. Earlier a hotel worker said the building, close to the French embassy, had been badly hit but there were no reports of casualties.
Witnesses said an estimated 400 rebels had joined the attack and at least two had been killed.
French troops in the former colony have been protecting the presidential palace and other key sites in the capital but until now had not intervened in the fighting.
They used helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles to quell a bloodier army uprising in May.
Residents said mutineers based in the Kassai barracks on the eastern outskirst of town used mortars and other heavy weapons for the first time. Rebels control the barracks and the main armoury there.

The mutiny, which began on November 16 and is the third this year, has shifted from grievances over pay and status to rebel demands for the resignation of elected President Ange-Felix Patasse. Tribal disputes are also at the root of the conflict.
Rebels reiterated on Tuesday they would not return to barracks until they have disarmed civilians and African mercenaries from Chad and Sudan backing Patasse.
"The president is the cause of tribal hatred," rebel spokesman Captain Anicet Saulet told BBC French service radio.
The mutiny has divided the city into a rebel-held south and west, and a northern and central area controlled by loyalists or French troops based in Bangui under bilateral accords.
Patasse's spokesman Prosper Douba this week accused rebels of holding the entire population hostage and of staging a coup.
Patasse decreed a night curfew on Bangui last week and repeated his call on mutineers to lay down their weapons unconditionally.
